title: InvestED, in order: a Rule #1 course
source: InvestED: The Rule #1 Podcast (Phil Town and Danielle Town), https://feeds.megaphone.fm/investedpodcast

modules.title: Orientation
modules.goal: Why Rule #1 investing, who's teaching, and how the course works.
modules.lesson:
1. **Retirement is a numbers problem you can't outsource to hope.** A typical plan is mostly the house plus a fund returning ~6%; after inflation it can run dry in about five years of drawing income, whereas the same savings at 15% changes the outcome ([029](episodes/029.md)).
2. **Compounding works both ways.** Inflation shrinks spending power and salaries lag it; debt compounds against you too ([030](episodes/030.md)).
3. **The best hedge is owning businesses with pricing power:** a moat lets a company raise prices with inflation.
4. **Manage your own money for three reasons:** moral, financial (you should do better) and practical (it isn't rocket science). Investing is a daily practice, like yoga, that you never finish ([065](episodes/065.md)).
5. **Patience is only possible with your own capital.** Fund managers are judged quarterly and can't sit in cash; you can.
6. Rule #1 (don't lose money) still frames everything; the retirement maths is *why* it matters.

modules.title: Understand the business
modules.goal: Circle of competence, the three circles, reading 10-Ks, and investing in line with your values.
modules.lesson:
Munger's four filters run in order, and **understanding** comes first: if you can't understand the business, stop.

1. **Find ideas without throwing darts.** Events, great investors' buys and the products you already use point you somewhere. They are tips, never decisions ([001](episodes/001.md), [011](episodes/011.md), [016](episodes/016.md)). Finding names is now easy; understanding is the filter ([077](episodes/077.md)).
2. **Start inside your circles** ([076](episodes/076.md)): overlap what you love, what you're world-class at and where you make and spend money. Check the company is public.
3. **Ignorance is the risk.** Related experience transfers (skiing to snowboarding), so start from humility, not self-doubt ([078](episodes/078.md), [079](episodes/079.md)).
4. **Wait for a fat pitch** and sort every candidate: too hard, no, wonderful but not on sale (watch list), or wonderful and on sale.
5. **Run the root-canal test:** if reading about the business is fun, you can learn it. Use the product, read its history, then the 10-K ([017](episodes/017.md)).
6. **Concentrate and dig your canyon.** Few businesses studied hard (scuttlebutt plus filings) beat many studied lightly.
7. **Test what you know.** Write a short white paper and invite corrections ([085](episodes/085.md)).
8. **Run any fashionable asset through the same list.** Phil does this with Bitcoin: he doesn't understand it, sees no moat or trustworthy managers and has no cash flow to price, so it is speculation ([135](episodes/135.md)).
9. **Check your values** and respect the edge: losses happen at the boundary of your competence.
10. **Finish with the next question:** what is the moat, and do the numbers show it?

modules.title: Moats
modules.goal: The five moats (brand, secret, toll bridge, switching, price), how to spot a durable competitive advantage, and how to tell when it's eroding.
modules.lesson:
1. **A moat is an *intrinsic*, *durable* advantage** (Buffett's water around the castle): remove it and the business suffers; rivals with the whole market cap still couldn't win ([003](episodes/003.md)). It is necessary, not sufficient.
2. **Six kinds** ([080](episodes/080.md), [088](episodes/088.md)): brand, toll bridge, price (*lowest cost*, not low price), switching, secrets (patents) and network effect. Earlier notes list five; network effect is a subset of switching. Companies can stack several.
3. **Moats are breachable.** Few companies from 1900 survive. Technology is hard because of creative destruction. Copying erodes them: Whole Foods lost its brand and secret edge once Kroger added organic ranges ([116](episodes/116.md)); USG's brand earns a price premium yet overcapacity wrecked returns ([113](episodes/113.md)).
4. **Scuttlebutt first:** talk to staff and customers, read the bears and ask competitors why they differ ([080](episodes/080.md)).
5. **Two tests** ([081](episodes/081.md), [082](episodes/082.md)): the numbers (ROE about 10% or better, free cash flow ÷ revenue) and an *obvious* moat. If you must strain to see it, it is too hard. Numbers look out of the back window, and obvious moats are already expensive ([110](episodes/110.md)).
6. **State it in a sentence.** If the 10-K and CEO can't point to the moat, don't invent one ([102](episodes/102.md)). Apparel shows the range: Patagonia's rests on real use by experts, Under Armour's team deals are only marketing ([105](episodes/105.md)).
7. **Replication test:** could you spend the purchase price and build a rival? A moat should survive an idiot, and shouldn't walk out the door with a star ([088](episodes/088.md)).

modules.title: Management
modules.goal: Owner-oriented, honest and capable leaders, and how to judge them from letters, calls and capital allocation.
modules.lesson:
1. **Integrity means integrated:** what you see is what you get. Talent is mainly **capital allocation**: reinvest, acquire, pay out or buy back ([005](episodes/005.md), [100](episodes/100.md)). Think like a sole owner.
2. **Management is where you can still lose everything.** A moat protects against an idiot, not a clever bad actor who loads the company with debt ([089](episodes/089.md), [117](episodes/117.md), [127](episodes/127.md)). Character shows under pressure ([107](episodes/107.md)).
3. **Debt is the real danger** (Horsehead, [075](episodes/075.md)). Years to repay from free cash flow: three at most, and falling ([089](episodes/089.md), [090](episodes/090.md)); [123](episodes/123.md) prefers one to two. Debt also lets managers use bankruptcy to take control.
4. **ROE flattered by debt:** swap equity for borrowing and ROE rises while ROIC doesn't. If ROIC falls relative to ROE, debt is creeping up ([123](episodes/123.md)).
5. **Follow the incentives** ([126](episodes/126.md)). Bonuses tied to short tenures, dilution, reverse splits and voting preferred shares (DryShips) show where owners rank.
6. **Six warning signs** ([089](episodes/089.md)): pay tied to asset size, little own money in the stock, value-destroying acquisitions, shares sold below stated value, a puff-piece letter and EBITDA treated as cash ([102](episodes/102.md)).
7. **Buybacks and acquisitions pass one test:** buy only below value ([100](episodes/100.md)).
8. **If you can't meet them, use clues** ([126](episodes/126.md), [127](episodes/127.md)): a founder or owner with a big stake who loves the business, no debt, and great investors with access buying, not quickly leaving. If two people decide everything (Sears), it is too hard.
9. **Control cuts both ways.** Dual-class shares protect a good founder and shield a poor one ([107](episodes/107.md)).
10. **Refinement:** management matters *less* than the business ([053](episodes/053.md)); [123](episodes/123.md) weights it slightly less for mature moats than for ventures (jockey versus horse), yet it holds a veto. Stay out of insurers and banks unless it's your field ([102](episodes/102.md)).

modules.title: The numbers: Big Five and ROIC
modules.goal: ROIC, sales, EPS, equity (BVPS) and operating cash flow growth, plus debt, and what they reveal about a moat.
modules.lesson:
1. **ROE (profit ÷ equity) of 10%+ for ten years, not falling, with no debt** is the first proof of a moat ([004](episodes/004.md)). Ten years is long enough for competitors to attack.
2. **Later refinement: ROIC** (return on all invested capital, debt included) is the better number; with no debt, ROE and ROIC match, so Phil simplifies to *avoid debt* ([021](episodes/021.md), [022](episodes/022.md)).
3. **The big four growth rates:** equity (book value) per share, EPS, sales and operating cash flow per share. Look for each at about 10%+ a year and *moving together* ([019](episodes/019.md), [020](episodes/020.md)). Tangled lines (General Motors) mean too hard.
4. **Operating cash flow is the canary** that catches accounting fictions first; EPS is partly a "fiction" of accruals.
5. **Know where each number comes from** ([068](episodes/068.md)): free cash flow isn't a GAAP figure, so two sites can differ (Netflix's DVD library). Go to the 10-K and read the notes on odd lines.
6. **The numbers are rear-view.** They show a moat existed; you still must understand why it will last ([023](episodes/023.md)).
7. **Score a real case** ([043](episodes/043.md)): Chipotle against seven numbers. Tech is mostly avoided because moats there erode fast ([022](episodes/022.md)).

modules.title: Valuation and margin of safety
modules.goal: Sticker Price, the MOS price, Payback Time, Ten Cap and the reasoning behind each.
modules.lesson:
1. **Price is what you pay, value is what you get** ([006](episodes/006.md)). Value is cash that reaches the owner; earnings are accrual fiction. Use **free cash flow** (operating cash flow minus purchase of property and equipment) and test it against net income over ten years: about 100% or more is ideal ([069](episodes/069.md), [095](episodes/095.md)). Whole Foods made ~$800M of FCF on $507M of earnings ([119](episodes/119.md)).
2. **The chain in one line** ([121](episodes/121.md)): grow EPS ten years, apply a P/E, discount at the 15% MARR (divide by about 4), then halve. The **windage** growth rate is judgement across 5, 7 and 10 years of the big four, not an average.
3. **Sticker price, four inputs** ([009](episodes/009.md), [024](episodes/024.md), [054](episodes/054.md)): trailing EPS, ten-year growth (lower of yours and analysts'), future P/E (lower of twice growth or historical high), 15% MARR.
4. **Quick and dirty** ([093](episodes/093.md)): check the growth rates run in parallel, trust trends over a year, treat analyst growth as a ceiling ([122](episodes/122.md)).
5. **Buy at half the sticker price** ([010](episodes/010.md), [058](episodes/058.md)); Buffett now accepts 20-40% off. Discounts need a trigger from the credit cycle or a company problem ([121](episodes/121.md)).
6. **Payback time:** about eight years at most ([008](episodes/008.md), [059](episodes/059.md)). The book used EPS, now FCF.
7. **Ten cap** ([146](episodes/146.md)): owner cash flow x 10 is a fair price, a 10% yield (a cap rate, as for a house). It assumes a moat and honest managers. Discounted cash flow is avoided because the growth rate is unknowable; the ten cap, the sticker price and a free-cash-flow method triangulate.
8. **Reverse-engineer a price:** find the growth it implies. $42 for Whole Foods needed ~16% against analysts' 6% ([122](episodes/122.md)).
9. **Checklist** ([071](episodes/071.md)): two of three methods say on sale, a guru is buying, an event with a 1-3 year cause.
10. **Dividends are not an input** ([066](episodes/066.md)). **Values veto, they don't discount** ([044](episodes/044.md)).

modules.title: Events and buying
modules.goal: Waiting for a business to go on sale, events, buying in tranches and building a watchlist.
modules.lesson:
1. **Mr. Market is moody; you may ignore him** and buy when fear puts a good business on sale ([007](episodes/007.md)). Volatility is not risk.
2. **A good event is temporary and fixable,** at a business you understand and priced clearly below value ([025](episodes/025.md)). A fall that isn't an event is no sale.
3. **System-wide events** (an election, a crash) move price without changing value ([083](episodes/083.md)). Don't trade the vote. Diversification doesn't help in a falling tide; use the fear to see whether watch-list names reach a margin-of-safety price.
4. **RULERS** ([012](episodes/012.md)): Radar, Understand, Love, Event, Reduce basis, Story.
5. **Radar has five sources** ([077](episodes/077.md)): scanning tools, gurus' 13F filings, brokers, friends and newsletters or research sites. Each gives only a name, to be run through the four filters. Beware inside information.
6. **Buy in tranches** as the price falls, and keep cash as an advantage. Be *anti-fragile*: the investor needs events.
7. **Whole-market gauges** (Wilshire 5000 to GDP) only tell you how hard to hunt, not when ([039](episodes/039.md), [083](episodes/083.md)).
8. **Invert the story:** write the bear case first. A drop after buying tests whether you understood.

modules.title: Psychology and practice
modules.goal: Fear, greed, patience, the tension signal, inversion and avoiding noise.
modules.lesson:
1. **Know what you don't know.** Use a margin of safety for errors you can't foresee ([047](episodes/047.md)). Simple is not easy ([087](episodes/087.md)).
2. **Fear drives mass diversification** ([057](episodes/057.md)). The middle path is about 10 companies (20 in a lifetime), 5-10% each, never over ~20%.
3. **Volatility is not risk** ([048](episodes/048.md), [035](episodes/035.md), [104](episodes/104.md), [114](episodes/114.md)). Managers are rational inside quarterly incentives; an owner of the cash flow need not sell. A crash is certain, so size for a 50% fall.
4. **Behavioural traps** ([108](episodes/108.md), [115](episodes/115.md)): sunk cost, endowment effect, loss aversion, anchoring, confirmation bias. Antidotes: a checklist, a "Munger" to argue the other side, saying the case aloud, staying in your circle.
5. **How afraid should you be?** Market cap to GDP ~140% and Shiller P/E ~29 say expensive ([106](episodes/106.md)), though Buffett says rates matter most ([113](episodes/113.md)). Learners build cash and a watchlist. Those who won't learn should index.
6. **Certainty is degrees** ([067](episodes/067.md)).
7. **Practise before money:** paper trade, size by conviction ([014](episodes/014.md), rerun [139](episodes/139.md)). An individual's edge is that nobody forces action ([062](episodes/062.md)).
8. **Investing is mostly a head game** ([131](episodes/131.md)): name the goal as a number and what the money is for, ask despite rejection, and find an hour a day for learning by trimming TV. Visualisation is motivation, not evidence.
9. **Separate fear from evidence** ([132](episodes/132.md)): after the research, fear at the buy is normal; ask whether the danger is real or imagined. Reading is the leader's habit. Tapping is Jack's unproven claim.
10. **Build your mindset like a muscle** ([096](episodes/096.md), [097](episodes/097.md), [137](episodes/137.md)): gratitude as a *practice* (firmer than a goal, looser than a promise), a calm mind before decisions, and intuition only as trained judgement.
11. **Shape your environment** and stay a student ([027](episodes/027.md), [074](episodes/074.md)).

modules.title: Portfolio and selling
modules.goal: Concentration, position sizing, when the story changes, and when to sell.
modules.lesson:
1. **Rank asset buckets by what they produce:** bonds are low risk and low return; gold and currency are hedges or too-hard bets ([036](episodes/036.md)); commodities have no moat ([037](episodes/037.md), [038](episodes/038.md)); annuities bet on your lifespan ([031](episodes/031.md)).
2. **Fees, taxes and misaligned incentives** destroy compounding in mutual funds ([015](episodes/015.md)). Robo-advisors automate modern portfolio theory cheaply ([049](episodes/049.md)).
3. **Passive versus active** ([130](episodes/130.md)): index funds cost ~0.1-0.25% against 1-2% and suit people who won't do the work. If everyone indexes, prices follow fund flows, so the market gets fragile, which helps a patient owner with cash.
4. **Diversified, leveraged portfolios** (Dalio's All Weather, [129](episodes/129.md)) protect assets already built; they are the wrong tool while you are still building. A gold ETF is an IOU inside the market.
5. **Risk, two definitions** ([094](episodes/094.md)): beta versus company risk; market-wide moves are weather.
6. **Real estate follows the same rules;** a REIT adds liquidity ([034](episodes/034.md)).
7. **Reduce basis** ([026](episodes/026.md)): dividends return capital until the holding acts like a growing "equity bond". A dividend is only as safe as owner cash flow and low debt ([028](episodes/028.md), [066](episodes/066.md)).
8. **Wait for the fat pitch** ([124](episodes/124.md)): like Ted Williams, swing only in your best zone. Fund managers must keep swinging; you needn't, and cash is capital for a great pitch. Narrow the zone if time is short; build the watch list now.
9. **Cash is a position** ([072](episodes/072.md)). Be slow in research and quick in buying, with a washtub, not a thimble. Reallocate only when a clearly better pitch appears.
10. **Wait** when markets are stretched (about 130% of GDP).

modules.title: The masters
modules.goal: Buffett, Munger, Graham, Pabrai, Spier and others: their ideas and their records.
modules.lesson:
1. **Dhandho** ([013](episodes/013.md)): asymmetric bets, small loss if wrong, large gain if right; Pabrai's "free lottery tickets" ([098](episodes/098.md), [099](episodes/099.md)).
2. **Size by conviction;** diversification is for those who don't know ([099](episodes/099.md)).
3. **Graham to Munger** ([063](episodes/063.md), [098](episodes/098.md), [141](episodes/141.md)): Graham held 100-200 bargains and was always invested; Buffett and Munger wait for a few wonderful businesses on sale.
4. **Keep learning and change your mind** ([099](episodes/099.md)).
5. **Leverage and forced selling cut both ways** (Guerin, Berkowitz).
6. **Patience is the individual's edge** ([101](episodes/101.md), [120](episodes/120.md), [144](episodes/144.md)): Pabrai's portfolio is mostly cash; institutions can't sit out.
7. **Read the letters and meetings** ([101](episodes/101.md), [112](episodes/112.md), [113](episodes/113.md)).
8. **How to use gurus** ([138](episodes/138.md), [141](episodes/141.md), [143](episodes/143.md)): curate a short list of concentrated value investors (Phil's has ~46) and read 13Fs through a site that shows quarterly change, not raw EDGAR. Filings lag up to 45 days; a 5% stake is reported within days. Big funds buy slowly, so a position may have taken months to build.
9. **What a 13F hides** ([140](episodes/140.md), [144](episodes/144.md)): cash, shorts and hedges. Know each manager's method (turnaround, deep value, long/short) before copying.
10. **Read the pattern** ([143](episodes/143.md), [145](episodes/145.md)): top five holdings of 50%+, small *practice shares*, and gurus rarely overlap. Their buying is a clue to reopen a "no", then do your own work, since you must know whether to hold in a 50% fall.
11. **You don't need money to start** ([145](episodes/145.md)): paper trade and keep a watch list.
12. **Model, don't copy** ([086](episodes/086.md)). The Spier reruns ([109](episodes/109.md), [111](episodes/111.md)) add only a hiatus note.
13. **Speculation versus investing** ([042](episodes/042.md)): does the return hold if nothing wonderful happens?

modules.title: Case studies and interviews
modules.goal: Companies analysed on the show, and guests' stories and lessons.
modules.lesson:
1. **Real assets obey Rule #1** ([033](episodes/033.md)): understand them, find a durable edge (location), buy after a bust. Buffett's Nebraska farm and New York building combine a cash-flow return, a bust seller and a margin of safety.
2. **Specialists beat generalists;** break the overwhelming into small steps and use scuttlebutt.
3. **A real loss, dissected** ([075](episodes/075.md)): Horsehead had a cost moat but a short management record and rising debt. **Debt kills.**
4. **Run the filters on a name** ([103](episodes/103.md), [105](episodes/105.md)): Under Armour has an okay moat and negative free cash flow; Lululemon's ten cap says wait. Treat each pick as one of 20 punches.
5. **Whole Foods, start to finish** ([116](episodes/116.md), [118](episodes/118.md), [119](episodes/119.md), [125](episodes/125.md)): moat erosion, an activist, Amazon's $42. On deal day Amazon's price cuts and a three-day grocer sell-off showed a price moat is fragile against a rival that can lose money; a brand moat counts only if it earns pricing power in the margins. A founder may pick a buyer by values.
6. **Disruptors fail the tools** ([128](episodes/128.md)): Tesla has no earnings and no ten-year history, so it is too hard, however loved. Loving a product is no margin of safety. Fund such bets separately, angel-style, after the plain work. Disruption can also hit "safe" holdings.
7. **Crypto is speculation** ([133](episodes/133.md), [134](episodes/134.md), [136](episodes/136.md)): no cash flow means no value to discount; the Picasso test and tulip mania apply. Blockchain, a shared ledger, is investable through companies; ICOs often need only a white paper, so check the team, and most are garbage.
8. **Check the ten-year history** you are asked for; don't explain red flags away.
9. **Your money is a vote** ([056](episodes/056.md)): Phil prescribes no set of values. Wealth is more than money ([142](episodes/142.md)).

glossary.definition: Don't lose money. Rule #2: don't forget Rule #1 (Buffett).
Meaning (understand it), Moat, Management, Margin of safety: Munger's four filters, applied in order.
The set of businesses you truly understand. Knowing where it ends matters more than how big it is.
Temporary bad news that puts a good business on sale.
Buying far enough below value (Rule #1: 50% of Sticker) that mistakes don't lose you money.
Making the best case against your idea, then rebutting it or walking away.
Buffett's thought experiment: only 20 purchases in a lifetime, so each must count.
Ideas you pass on because you can't understand them well enough.
A durable competitive advantage: brand, secrets, switching, toll bridge or low cost.
Return on equity: profit divided by shareholders' equity. Rule #1 wants 10%+ for ten years.
Return on invested capital: profit on all capital, debt included. Better than ROE once debt is in play.
Equity (book value), EPS, sales and operating cash flow per share, each ideally growing 10%+ together.
Phil's estimate of value today: grow EPS ten years, apply a future P/E, discount at 15%.
Minimum acceptable rate of return: 15% a year in Rule #1.
Years of cash flow needed to earn back the price paid. About eight or fewer is a fair price.
Net earnings minus maintenance capex: the cash an owner could take out.
First-year cash return on purchase price; the price test for real estate and cash-flow businesses.
Graham's moody business partner who quotes a price daily; you may ignore him.
The theory that price already reflects all information. Rule #1 relies on it failing in the short run.
Modern portfolio theory calls price movement risk; Rule #1 says a falling price on unchanged value lowers risk.
Lower the money at risk in a holding by taking cash back, such as dividends.
A business whose cash payout to you grows over time, like a bond whose coupon keeps rising.
Radar, Understand, Love, Event, Reduce basis, Story: Phil's checklist.
A narrow area you study deeply: an inch wide and a mile deep.
Gathering information from customers, employees, suppliers and competitors.
Gujarati for endeavours that create wealth: low-risk, high-uncertainty bets (Pabrai).
Real estate investment trust: a listed company owning property that passes income to shareholders.
A contract paying income for life; essentially a bet on your lifespan that inflation erodes.
Cash generated by running the business; catches accounting fictions first.
Ability to raise prices without losing customers; the inflation hedge.
Valuing a holding at today's quoted price rather than its value.
Cash from operations minus purchase of property and equipment; the cash left for owners. Not a GAAP number, so sources differ.
Years to double ≈ 72 ÷ annual return in percent; also the quick way to discount a future value.
Tangible book value (equity minus goodwill and intangibles): what the business is worth dead. Taught in 060, later dropped as a method.
Graham's very cheap, low-quality company that gives one last puff of profit; Munger steered Buffett to wonderful businesses instead.
The latest four quarters combined; the earnings base for the sticker price.
The pressure on professional managers to match the crowd and show results every quarter, so they cannot wait in cash.
Purchase price minus cash already returned (dividends); shows the risk still outstanding.
Buying something dear in the hope that someone else will pay more; the logic of bubbles.
Investing a fixed sum on a schedule regardless of price; Phil calls it a bet that the market rises.
Buffett's borrowed baseball idea: there are no called strikes, so wait for an obvious opportunity inside the zone you understand.
A moat where the only alternative is far costlier, usually a physical or regulatory monopoly (railroad lines, utilities). Hard to hold without regulation.
Being the lowest-cost producer, so you survive price wars and troughs that shut others down. Matters most in commodity businesses.
How much a stock tends to move relative to the market (1.0 = the market). Modern portfolio theory's measure of risk; Phil ignores it.
Taleb's term for something that gains from shocks. Rule #1 investing needs panics to buy wonderful companies on sale.
Years of free cash flow needed to repay the debt. About three at most, and falling.
Ask whether reading about a business and its industry is fun or a root canal; fun suggests you can learn it.
Earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization. Buffett and Munger call it a delusion because it ignores real costs of keeping the business running.
The growth rate you choose by judgement after studying all four growth numbers over 5, 7 and 10 years, not a simple average.
Buffett's image of holding cash for the storm that rains gold: a bucket, not a thimble.
Owning something makes you value it above what you would pay for it, so selling feels like a loss.
Money already spent is gone either way and should not change whether you hold or sell.
Buying a stock trading below a takeover price to collect the gap: speculation with an edge, not Rule #1 investing.
Share classes with unequal votes that give founders or families control; check what voting power you are buying.
Total US stock value divided by GDP; Buffett called 70-80% fine and 100% playing with fire.
Clinging to a price or past view after the facts change; the cure is to recheck your homework.
Quick valuation: free cash flow times 10 (a 10% cash yield) as a rough fair market cap.
Fewer shares, each worth proportionally more; changes nothing by itself but is often used after steep falls and dilution (DryShips).
A stock bought because its assets are worth more than its price; it depends on management realising the value (Sears).
A low-cost fund that copies an index (about 0.1-0.25% a year against 1-2% for active funds); Buffett's advice for those who won't learn to invest.
A ledger shared across many computers so records are hard to change; the technology is investable through companies, a coin is not.
Initial coin offering: a sale of new tokens, often on only a white paper.
Buying for a price rise without a way to value the asset's cash flow (Bitcoin, a Picasso, tulips).
Quarterly report of long US stock holdings by managers with over $100 million; up to 45 days late and silent on cash and shorts.
Borrowing shares, selling them and hoping to buy back cheaper; losses are theoretically unlimited.
A long/short pairing meant to profit whichever way the market moves; hard because it needs two right answers.
A fund holding longs and shorts, so its 13F overstates its exposure.
A tiny position used to force yourself to follow a company while you learn it.
Phil's concentration test: the top five holdings should be at least about half the portfolio.
A tradable right to buy shares at a fixed price before an expiry date; it carries a clock.
